items.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: it’s ironic that my business partner and my best friend, Stanley, was probably with Buddy in Binghamton when I was eleven.

ctx.x: Right, I was going to ask about that.

First I started in college at SUNY Binghamton, the state university — I started at Ithaca then I finished at SUNY and Al liked the way I played and subsequently I went into all of his bands, and he booked a lot of the shows in Binghamton and I played all the time there. It was like the best possible way to train to do anything in music was to be playing in his big bands and his small bands and he introduced me to Slam Stewart and I played with Slam a lot and got to play on Slam’s last album with him, and Al…

came through town, every show, I played percussion for all of them. So it was phenomenal. So that was that phase of my life. But really somebody who opened my eyes unbelievably to music was Stanley Kay when I came to New York in 1986. I met him a few years later and he’s like to me a genius and so inspirational to me, not just about music, but the music business, about drumming, about jazz, about big band playing.

items.title: Stanley Kay interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001
items.q: represent Sherrie and our band in the best way possible... what Sherrie, the reaction to Sherrie and Nicki and Karolina and Anat. Because they are fine musicians.

ctx.x: Yeah. How did it work with being in with Buddy Rich. He played part of the time?

No. What it was, see it’s a fallacy. People write what they think. They think that I drove the bus, which I never did because I couldn’t ride a bicycle. I didn’t drive any bus. I could drive a car. What it was is I was his assistant so to speak. In other words they said that I went and played the charts and he sat when we got a new chart, that he sat in front listening to me play. That’s not true. Because when he was with Tommy, Harry James, Artie Shaw, there was no assistant drummer. He could play it the first…

contributed a lot to jazz.” And everybody in the audience in listening. They’ve got their ears up. And they says, “you don’t know this, but he was the original drummer of ‘How Much is that Doggie in the Window’ with Patti Page.” And I was.
